biome.def: A large region of the Earth with a typical climate and typical plants and animals, such as tundra, desert or tropical rainforest. The same biome can occur on several continents.

precipitation.def: Water that falls from the atmosphere as rain, snow, sleet or hail, usually measured in centimeters or millimeters.

climatograph.def: A graph of a place’s average temperature and precipitation for each month of the year, used to identify its biome.

tropical-rainforest.def: A biome near the equator that is warm and very wet all year (often over 200 cm of rain), with dense, layered forest and soils poor in nutrients.

temperate-forest.def: A temperate deciduous forest: a biome with warm summers, cold winters and rain through the year, whose broadleaf trees drop their leaves in fall.

temperate-rainforest.def: A coastal biome with mild temperatures and very heavy rain from ocean air, with huge conifers, mosses and ferns.

taiga.def: The boreal forest: a cold biome of cone-bearing evergreen trees with long, snowy winters and short summers, just south of the tundra.

tundra.def: A cold, treeless biome with long winters, a short growing season, little precipitation and permafrost, found at high latitudes and on high mountains.

permafrost.def: Soil that stays frozen all year. It lies under the tundra, keeps roots shallow and stores large amounts of dead plant matter.

savanna.def: A tropical grassland with scattered trees, warm all year, with a wet season and a long dry season; fires and grazing keep it open.

temperate-grassland.def: A biome of grasses and few trees with hot summers, cold winters and moderate precipitation, such as a prairie. Its deep soils are very fertile for farming.

desert-biome.def: A biome that gets very little precipitation (usually under 25 cm a year), with plants that store water; it can be hot or cold.

chaparral.def: A shrubland biome with hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters, where shrubs with small waxy leaves grow and fires are common.
